utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Registrar, have General Blaskic brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume where we stopped off with the last testimony. I think it is time for the cross-examination. We have a very busy schedule. Can the interpreters hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can the witness hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you rested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you feeling well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are going to listen to questions put to you by Mr. Nobilo, who is Defence counsel for General Blaskic. WITNESS JJ (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will try to be very brief today. Good afternoon, Witness JJ

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was it true that you were mobilised -- when the war in Sarajevo started, was there a general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were called by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, I am referring to the Bosnian army, which was called the Patriotic League and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was mobilised into the Patriotic League and later joined the military police, as I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When asked by the Prosecution about what you did after you left the Patriotic League, you said that you had village watches -- what kind of a set-up was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how to explain this. We were with the Croats, with our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So are you saying that this was a self-organised thing, something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, self-organisation by both the Croats and us, and this was by individual villagers and only at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you were not an army; you were just night watchers and, other than that, you were just simple civilians and citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And how long did this go on -- until you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, these night watches went on until the deterioration of the situation in (redacted) This had to do with the taking of the barracks in (redacted) and the flying of the chequer board flag and then no Muslims were involved any more and that is the time when these joint watches stopped being taken, and we would only meet at the end of the night in the edge of the villages of (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you parted with Croats, was there a change in your status -- did you then become a part of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or were you just simply a village watch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were only the village watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And you remained the village watch until the HVO came to your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, can we please go into the private session for a moment, because I would like to avoid identifying the witness, because I want to ask some question about his personal data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor -- Mr. Registrar -- are you talking about a private session? (In private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (In public session)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can I please have the exhibit number from the Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is D111 -- A for the French version and B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned two factions in the HVO. One was led by Rajic and the other by Lujo. Can we say these two factions existed as early as spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about the date of the month, but I know they existed. I do not know when this Lujo exactly died and his bodyguard Marko, but I am aware they existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am going to read to you what you stated to the investigator of the Prosecution and on page 3 of the English text, it states: "... in spring 1993, one day Lujo arrested Ivica Rajic and kept him in prison for three days." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. And Rajic was the chief commander of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me about (redacted) -- is it true that he was trying to protect you from being robbed, or any other problems in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it correct that the reason why he told you to stay inside your houses was for your own protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me, you said that you heard weapons firing. How long did this go on -- I mean in the surrounding villages, because there was no fighting in your village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, the first day, we could hear it well, and the next day as well, but not as much as the first morning, and at that time I was not in a position where I could see or hear so well, because we had withdrawn into a forest, and we could not hear it so well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So it could be heard for two days. Can you say from which directions, from the direction of which villages you heard that gun fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The small arms fire started (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Is it also correct what you stated before that (redacted) also secured food to you which was the same food as the one for the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is true in regards to (redacted) and when he was around.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was there, no, but later on, after I went to the barracks, when I was exchanged, the rumour was (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You also mentioned (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I must object at this point. The witness did not make any reference to (redacted) I have the transcript with me now. If Mr. Nobilo wants to look through it he will find there is (redacted) (redacted). It is outside the scope of the examination-in-chief and I would ask him to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am going to read a portion of the statement. I said that it was in the statement. On page 12 of the Croat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But what are we talking about, please? Are we talking about the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, no, we are talking about the statement which the witness gave to the OTP, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but the Prosecutor did not refer to it in the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination has to refer to the examination-in-chief. The rule is flexible. I know that. Mr. Hayman wants to say something, but I must remind you that a ruling was taken by the Chamber and applied in a flexible manner, but you have the floor, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a clear recollection of Mr. Cayley, in his introduction of this witness, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Unfortunately, your Honour, Mr. Hayman is being economical with the truth. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (redacted) I referred to an incident, but I certainly did not make any reference to that group. I simply repeat again, the rules under which I am operating are that the cross-examination is limited to my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. In that case,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Nobilo, put your question but avoid the word (redacted) -- you can refer to the incident -- that is what I would suggest to you. It may be a bit difficult, but try -- just a single question and let us go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. I will not mention the word (redacted), but this unit -- from whom did it receive orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We know well who was in this unit, and they did most evil. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) This unit today does not control things, but certain individuals from this unit still control this area and the roads and communication lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But tell me, during the war, who did they recognise as their commander -- who did they receive orders from during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From conversation (redacted), and the Croats who came after the conflict, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How do your neighbours know from whom (redacted) received orders -- were they present on any occasion when --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I was a member of the BiH army, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But you were not in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, during your stay in (redacted), in all the events that you described, have you ever -- did you ever meet (redacted) -- you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When was this (redacted) rally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly. I cannot say exactly the month, but we know when the (redacted) was established, and when the (redacted) was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But this must have been before these conflicts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That is all the questions we have of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have only a few questions, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This does not mean that you can speak about (redacted) now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The first request I have is this document that was admitted by the Defence be placed under seal, together with that relevant portion of the evidence. Otherwise the witness will be identified from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Of course, in order to protect the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, the unit that is indicated on this card that was presented to you by the Defence, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: My colleague is asking me whether we are in a private session or not. We are in a public session -- I wish to remind you of that, Mr. Cayley. Is that going to cause any problems, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it crossed my mind, but frankly there must have been a large number of people in this unit. I do not think it will necessarily identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection then. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you answer that question that I just put to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He answered it. It is in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I did not hear it, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The answer was "no".

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether this was on paper, but, first of all, (redacted) (redacted) Most probably because this unit involved (redacted) -- it is obvious that all the able-bodied persons were on that list, but, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You mentioned, both in your examination-in-chief and your cross-examination, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) He tried to protect us from it, but, because the (redacted) members came from (redacted) his name was (redacted) and they wanted us to go over there and dig trenches. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (redacted), how were you treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were treated much worse than when he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By "much worse", what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean that we had to work much harder, the food was poorer. As far as conditions are concerned, whether it rained or the sun shown, without regard to the weather conditions, we would have to dig, whereas he would tell us to take shelter, take rest, light a cigarette, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But (redacted) was still the individual who took you every day to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, (redacted) was in fact not the person who was taking us there. He was the commander of -- I do not know how that unit was called -- the unit which was there at (redacted). He would simply send somebody in a vehicle. At first we went there on foot, because it was not that far from this front-line, and without any escort, because the (redacted) lines were all around us. We were told that the area around the (redacted) was mined, so this was near my house, so there was no place we could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You mentioned in your examination-in-chief and your cross-examination that it was common knowledge

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we knew that he was the commander, and that he received his orders and passed them on later, so that he received them (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this was common knowledge throughout

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever hear if there was a time when

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I just want to make sure that I noted properly what you said. Among other things, you said that an (redacted) came to cleanse the village under a commander. Was this a disciplined unit -- a disciplined armed unit? (redacted) (redacted); was this a disciplined armed unit, in your opinion, or was it just people coming to attack and to rob and frighten the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The unit turned out to be disciplined. First of all, we surrendered our weapons without firing a bullet -- not even lighted a match, and we were told that, if we did not surrender the arms, the village would be torched, that the women and children, the elderly, would all be killed, and we surrendered everything so that we would prevent this from happening, and, when we surrendered everything, two houses were set on fire, one belonged to a policeman who had already left the village and went to (redacted) so maybe they wanted him, maybe they wanted information from him, so they were not able to arrest him. So they set that house on fire -- even though we had surrendered weapons and offered no resistance and also a house of another man who had fled to (redacted) who found a way through the lines. I do not know if he was assisted by any Croats but he left in the evening and, in the morning, the house was burnt to the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So I gather this unit had all the characteristics of being a disciplined armed unit -- that is right, under a commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Under a responsible commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, this is how it was. I do not know how they would have behaved had we not surrendered weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you spoke also of (redacted) (redacted) What was his rank exactly, do you know? Was he more than a colonel or less than a colonel, or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not tell you the rank, but I am clear on one thing. I experienced -- my weapon was taken away from me (redacted). I was a military policeman and the (redacted) took away my weapon and told me to go to (redacted) in the (redacted). I went there, I reported, the police took me over to his office. I waited for about an hour, an hour and a half, to have a conversation and get my weapon back and then he said that he could not decide anything until he had discussed things (redacted) and, later, I was told that I would never get my weapon back and it was a good thing that I managed to get out. (redacted) (redacted) -- I complained to him and asked to be given this weapon back, but he said he was in such a position that he was just a simple soldier and he could not talk to him about such affairs, such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned you were often visited and mistreated by soldiers; were they also (redacted) soldiers, military or would they be people just being recruited from everywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were people from different places. When these people would come, we did not know them, so they would not hide, but if somebody from the neighbouring village came, they would put a stocking on their face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And they looked like soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only looked like soldiers, but they had the uniforms, the (redacted) insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I want to talk to you about (redacted) -- I think you said his name was (redacted) (redacted). I take it he was a Croat, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is a Croat, and his name is (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I want to confirm my understanding of your evidence to be this, that (redacted) would take you to dig trenches, but that he was protective of you and others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This man most probably would not have taken us to dig trenches. He proved to be a good neighbour, but I said that other people came from (redacted) These were men called (redacted) They came with a truck to dig. He wanted to protect us from mistreatment when digging elsewhere, so he kept us digging in his area so that we would be more protected under him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly then to mean that it was your impression at the time that he took you to dig trenches because he felt he had to take you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe he did not have to do this, but then we would have had to go somewhere else to dig, and, as the fighting kept spreading, as new front-lines were being taken, and this was done elsewhere -- people would go (redacted) for people to dig trenches, because only the prisoners dug trenches, not their own people, and later on I witnessed that this same (redacted) came to ask for 10 or 15 people to work on something in his own village, so, I do not know, the work had been incomplete, so he needed more for the evacuation of these front-lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just before these things happened, did you have friends (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I always had friends (redacted), and I have them to date. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: he came to my place and he apologised to me. He said that he did not know what he was doing, that he had to do it, that he had been ordered to personally beat me. So, today, I go to my (redacted) except I do it not -- I use a car with a foreign registration plate, not my own, so I stay with him and I see some other neighbours. We have remained on good terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, do

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there are quite a few such cases -- a lot of them, because a lot of (redacted) are not guilty -- they are not responsible for this (redacted) and such silly things, so some of them feel remorse now and they cannot understand why they attacked (redacted). For instance, when we meet in a cafe, they themselves cannot imagine how and why this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Can you tell the court a little about the kind of relations which now exist between (redacted) communities and (redacted) communities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relations are still not very good. If they were, everybody would be back at their -- in their own homes. We would have a joint army. We did not need to call it the (redacted) army. I said that it is still not safe to pass through certain places -- vehicles are still stopped, people put barrels of guns into people's mouths -- it is still unfathomable what is going on in (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One last question. You told us about (redacted) At the time when these events occurred, were there other (redacted) who were protective of (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could maybe mention another couple of people from my village, but from other places, no -- at least that I know of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness JJ. That brings to an end your testimony. The Tribunal wishes to thank you for coming here to evoke memories of this painful period in your life. I have no further questions for you. You are going to return home, and I hope you will be able to find peace of mind there. Do not move for the moment, because you are under protection. The Trial Chamber is going to rise. That is the end for this week, is it not, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to have a 10-minute break, and then we will have a closed session for an ex parte hearing with the Defence. Of course, that will be in the presence of the accused. We will now have a 10-minute break. (3.33pm)
